paragraphs: Every year, the Government writes a plan to fight climate change. This year's plan was due in January. Now it will come in November.
That is 11 months late. Last year's plan was also late, by four months. The Government says the new plan will be ready soon.
The plan will have 18 main areas. They include more wind farms at sea, more electric cars and better public transport.
Ireland wants to cut its pollution by 51% by 2030. But the climate minister, Darragh O'Brien, says this will probably not happen.
Some opposition parties are angry. They say the Government does not care enough about the climate. They want faster action.
sentZh: 政府每年都會撰寫一份對抗氣候變遷的計畫。
今年的計畫原定在一月推出。
現在要到十一月才會推出。
那晚了11個月。
去年的計畫也晚了四個月。
政府說新計畫很快就會準備好。
這份計畫將有18個主要領域。
包括更多海上風力發電場、更多電動車和更好的大眾運輸。
愛爾蘭希望在2030年前把污染減少51%。
但氣候部長達拉·奧布萊恩說，這可能不會實現。
一些反對黨很生氣。
他們說政府不夠重視氣候。
他們希望行動更快。

paragraphs: The Government's Climate Action Plan for 2026 will finally be approved by the Cabinet in November. It was supposed to come out in January, so it is 11 months late.

This is the second year in a row that the plan has been late. The 2025 plan came out in April, four months after it was due. Because the new plan is so late, it will probably also include the plan for 2027.

The plan is the Government's main guide for cutting greenhouse gases. It will have 18 priority areas, such as improving the electricity grid, building more offshore wind farms, getting more people into electric cars and reducing pollution from farming.
By law, Ireland must cut its emissions by 51% by 2030. However, Climate Minister Darragh O'Brien has already said that the country will probably miss this target.

Opposition parties say climate change is no longer a priority for the Government. Green Party leader Roderic O'Gorman said yearly plans are important because they let people check the Government's progress.
sentZh: 政府的2026年氣候行動計畫終於將在十一月由內閣批准。
它原本應該在一月推出，所以晚了11個月。
這是計畫連續第二年延遲。

這份計畫是政府減少溫室氣體的主要指南。
它將有18個優先領域，例如改善電網、建造更多離岸風力發電場、讓更多人改開電動車，以及減少農業污染。

paragraphs: The Government's Climate Action Plan for 2026, originally due in January, will be approved by Cabinet in November, an 11-month delay that has drawn criticism from opposition parties.

It is the second year in a row that the plan has been late; the 2025 version appeared in April, four months behind schedule. Given the timing, the new document is expected to incorporate the plan for 2027 as well.

The plan is the State's main roadmap for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. It will set out 18 priority areas, including upgrading the electricity grid, speeding up offshore wind projects, increasing the number of electric vehicles and decarbonising agriculture and industry.

Under climate law, Ireland is committed to cutting emissions by 51% by 2030 and becoming climate neutral by 2050. However, Minister for Climate Darragh O'Brien has admitted that the 2030 target is unlikely to be met.

Opposition parties argue that climate has been downgraded as a priority, pointing to support for data centres and the pausing of the carbon levy. Green Party leader Roderic O'Gorman said annual plans were essential for holding the Government to account.

paragraphs: The Government's long-overdue Climate Action Plan for 2026 will finally go before Cabinet in November, a full 11 months after its January deadline, prompting accusations that climate policy has slipped down the political agenda.
The delay eclipses last year's, when the 2025 plan surfaced in April, four months behind schedule. So belated is the latest edition that it is expected to subsume the 2027 plan as well.

Billed as the State's principal blueprint for curbing greenhouse gas emissions, the document will identify 18 priority areas, ranging from overhauling the electricity grid and streamlining offshore wind development to accelerating the uptake of electric vehicles and decarbonising farming and industry.
Ireland is legally bound to slash emissions by 51% by 2030 and to attain climate neutrality by 2050. Yet Minister for Climate Darragh O'Brien has conceded that the 2030 goal is all but out of reach.
